The Cyprus Arc is the active boundary where the Africa plate, to the south, is subducted beneath the Anatolian plate, to the north. It stretches NW-SE between the Dead Sea Fault, to the SE, and the Rhodes Basin, to the NW. Here this structure links with the Hellenic Arc.
The Cyprus subduction zone is probably the less known in the Mediterranean area. No well-defined volcanic arc exists. It seems to be evolving towards continental collision, at least in its eastern portion (Imprescia et al., 2012), as the crust in the Levantine Basin is not properly oceanic but more probably thinned continental. The accretionary wedge is in part deformed against the Eratostene Seamount, which is entering the deformation zone.
The eastern end of the Cyprus Arc is located against the Dead Sea Fault zone, which in turn ends against the eastern Anatolia Fault zone. At the opposite end, in the Rhodes Basin, the relationshipa with the Hellenic Arc are still the matter of debate, also for the unclear nature of the Cyprus subduction itself. The continuity of the subduction front is interrupted west of the Island of Cyprus by the right-lateral strike-slip Paphos Fault, which marks the boundary between the oceanic domain subducting to the west and the collision to the east.
According to GPS velocities and current plate models, the subducting Africa plate moves toward the NNW at 5-9 mm/y while the overriding Anatolian plate moves westward at 21 mm/y (both values are relative to fixed Eurasia; Reilinger et al., 2006). These relative motions result in a predominant orthogonal convergence at about 18 mm/y (Reilinger et al., 2006) or 14 mm/y in the western part of the arc, decreasing eastwards to 7-9 mm/y, where relative motion becomes oblique (Wdowinski et al., 2006). The subduction rate is estimated at about 10 mm/y by Agostini et al. (2010). The Paphos fault is thought to accommodate about 10 mm/y of differential velocity between east and west.
The seismicity distribution seems to depict a Wadati-Benioff zone beneath the Anatolia to a depth of about 140 km in the western part of the arc, while in its eastern portion no earthquakes are recorded beyond 60 km depth (Kalyoncuoglu et al., 2011).
The shallowest structures of the Cyprus Arc are imaged in the seismic lines interpreted by Vidal et al. (2000a, b and c), Woodside et al. (2002) and Benkhelil et al. (2005). Plate contact is clearly imaged only in the central portion of the arc, immediately south to the Cyprus Island (Vidal et al., 2000a; Schattner et al., 2010). The Bouguer gravity anomaly pattern seems to be consistent with the presence of a subducting slab down to 50 km depth and beyond (ErgÃƒÂ¼n et al., 2005). At greater depth only tomography data are available. A fast body seems to dip beneath Anatolia reaching a depth of about 400 km beneath the southern coast of the Black Sea. A deeper cold body is also imaged at depth between 400 and 800 km (Dilek and Sandvol, 2009). In the eastern portion of the Cyprus arc, a discontinuity in the cold body is interpreted as an indication of a slab detachment (Faccenna et al., 2006), possibly induced by the collision of the Eratostene Seamount with the Anatolia plate margin.
Seismic coupling estimates are not available for the Cyprus subduction (Heuret et al., 2011).
The Cyprus area has been affected by many destructive earthquakes known since historical times (Salamon et al., 2003; Cagnan and Tanircan, 2010). Part of them are ascribed (or could be, for those that lack an instrumental record) to crustal structures, such as the strike-slip Paphos fault, or thrust faults deforming the Anatolia plate margin (Papadimitriou et Karakostas, 2006). The largest known earthquakes in the Cyprus area may be those that occurred in 342 AD and on 11 May 1222, ranging in magnitude respectively between Mw 6.6 and 7.4 (CFTI4Med, Guidoboni et al., 2007; Cagnan and Tanircan, 2010) and between Mw 6.0 and 7.5 (CFTI4Med, Guidoboni et al., 2007; Guidoboni and Comastri, 2005; Yolsal et al., 2007).

pictures.c: Convergence rate between the pairs of plates Nubia and Anatolia and Sinai and Anatolia, calculated on geodetic basis. Note that values decrease eastwards (Wdowinski et al. [2006]).

Earthquakes hypocenters distribution seems to depict a Wadati-Benioff zone beneath the Anatolia to a depth of about 140 km in the western part of the arc, while in the eastern portion no earthquakes are recorded beyond 60-70 km depth (from Kalyoncuoglu et al. [2011]).
